doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

chapter: Dixieland and the college jazz scene
title: Album reissues and the records that formed his taste
summary: Reissue albums of Bix, Armstrong and Morton, new small-label records, and the Eddie Condon Saturday radio show.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Ten inch records, or in some cases twelve, mostly ten inch records, of eight Bix Beiderbecke things or eight sides of Armstrong or eight sides of Jelly Roll Morton.
Oh yeah, I see, when you say an album, you mean multiple records.
That’s right. Because Milt Fillius had given a bunch of those things. I forget that an album originally meant multiple records.

It was an album. These albums originally developed for classical music because if you wanted to have an opera, even on a twelve inch record, a twelve inch record is only going to play four and a half minutes of music on each side, nine minutes — if you’ve got an opera how many records are you going to need? So even if you excerpted them — or the

nine Beethoven symphonies that Toscanini did. These were in albums. They were in books with a hard cover and sleeves that, it was all together. So they began putting the jazz in these albums, these reissue programs. So we were listening, we were now ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen years old and we were listening to the Hot Fives and we were listening to Beiderbecke, we were listening to Morton, we were listening to Oliver, we were listening to the Ben Pollock Orchestra, you know, the band with Teagarden and Goodman, we were listening to all that stuff as well as the new records that were coming out, which were originally on Commodore, Blue Note, small labels of that kind, with Hackett, with Russell, with Teagarden, with Joe Sullivan, with Jess Stacy, with Davison and Brunies and all of these people who became our heroes. These were the heroes. And all through the United States, but particularly in the Northeast we had radio programs. We had the famous Eddie Condon Saturday afternoon from Town Hall, his program, so that kids all over and around the New York area, Saturday afternoon was sacred. You had to listen to the Eddie Condon show.
